sweep_summary: One bibliography item only: Smalley 1953 'Phonemic rhythm in Comanche' (IJAL 19(4):297-301, DOI 10.1086/464236). Its full text was already held by the project as the archive.., matching) and was re-read; the DOI landing page (journals.uchicago.edu) could not be reached by automated download and was not opened. Section 2 (p. 299) states that lexical stress is contrastive, occurs most prevalently on one of the first three syllables and most often on the first syllable of a root or compound; emphatic stress coincides with lexical stress, and lexical stress carries high pitch (sec. 4). This CONFIRMS the catalog's Charney-1993-based coding (initial default with lexically marked exceptions) and is silent on weight/mora counting, so the catalog's deciding source (Charney 1993) stands; Smalley 1953 is a supporting, not superseding, statement. Nothing remains to acquire for this item (priority none). Crossref record saved alongside.

new_statements.reading: Early first-hand (1949 fieldwork, Emily Riddles) description: Comanche word stress is phonemic/lexical, unpredictable in principle (minimal pairs), but with a strong default on the first syllable of the root or compound and confined to the first three syllables. This matches Charney 1993's 'most common position for stress is the first syllable; exceptions marked' and is silent on the weight/mora-counting detail (Charney p. 42 'every second mora rightward') on which the catalog's weight-hedged coding rests.

sources.quote: 2. The contrastive placing of lexical stress may be seen in the following words: 'tosahwI silver, wa'sape bear, mahto'koo thumb, kuyu'ni?nii turkeys, nimi'kuhcu? our (pl.) cow, 'nimikuhcu? buffalo. Emphatic stress, which occurs occasionally for affective purposes, always coincides in point of placement with lexical stress. [...] The distribution of lexical stress is most prevalent on one of the first three syllables of a word and most often on the first syllable of a root or compound.
sources.locator: sec. 2 'Lexically placed stress', p. 299 (first column); also fn. 2 p. 297 and sec. 4 p. 300
sources.note: Stress is phonemic and lexically placed (contrastive minimal pairs given, e.g. nimi'kuhcu? 'our cow' vs 'nimikuhcu? 'buffalo'); it falls most often on one of the first three syllables and most often on the first syllable of a root or compound. Lexical stress carries high pitch (sec. 4: 'high pitch on lexically stressed syllables and regular pitch elsewhere'); a separate utterance-level rhythm stress usually coincides with lexical stress but can suppress it. Nothing on syllable weight or mora counting; vowel length is analysed as VV sequences (sec. 3).
